newsitem.title: USA: US bill seen challenging Fed's payment system role.
newsitem.headline: US bill seen challenging Fed's payment system role.

text.p: A bill introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives may challenge the Federal Reserve's presence in the world's largest check-clearing and payments system, according to Fed sources.
Carolyn Maloney, D-NY, a member of the House Banking and Financial Services Committee, introduced "The Efficient Check-Clearing Act of 1997" in Congress on July 9.
Maloney's bill would alter an important feature of the law -- the Monetary Control Act of 1980 -- under which the Fed provides financial services to the public sector.

The Monetary Control Act requires the Fed to recover the overall costs of its financial services. The Act, however, does not ask the Fed to match individual costs and fees they collect for individual services.
This helps the Fed maintain its status as the nation's premier provider of comprehensive financial services.

"If the Fed were forced to fully price every single service, this could affect every area where the Fed operates," one Fed source in the payments system area told Reuters. "We'll probably get out of (the check-clearing) business all together."

Maloney's bill seeks the stand-alone recovery of all check transportation costs, "prohibiting the Fed from subsidizing the transportation of paper checks" and requesting the publication of check transportation fees.
"The Fed should not subsidize the transportation of paper checks. That's the purpose of my bill," Maloney told Reuters.

Maloney, who contended that her bill would save U.S. taxpayers millions of dollars every year, queried Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan on the issue during his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress last month.
Greenspan reassured Maloney that "for check services, as a group, we have recovered all (costs)" and that the Fed actually made a profit of about "$1 billion over the years."
But Maloney countered that a two-year study conducted by House Banking Committee's Democrats found that the Fed subsidized check transportation in numerous instances.
"The Democratic minority did a report that documented that was subsidized," Maloney stated.
The Fed charters about 60 planes to transport checks nationwide, including to remote areas where shipment costs are prohibitive for private competitors.

"The bill would want us to price transportation costs separately, to unbundle check transportation and collection," the source added. "One reason may be to make transportation services available to private-sector competitors."
The Fed's main competitor in the check shipment business is AirNet Systems Inc.

"If that bill were passed, you would see the Fed get out of the transportation business all together. The cost structure is such that the Fed can't compete. They would have to get out of the business or outsource it, which could be good for AirNet," an industry analyst told Reuters.
Another Fed source said Maloney's bill, if passed, would have broader implications for Fed operations.

"The Act requires us to cover overall costs, not specific subsets," one Fed official told Reuters. "If the law were to change, then the accounting method would change. This could apply to all our operations."

Maloney's bill comes at a time when the Fed is pondering its future role in the payments system, including check processing, automated transaction services, automated funds clearing and electronic funds transfers.

A commission led by Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin recently made public five possible scenarios involving the Fed's future in the payments system -- from ending its role altogether to becoming a leader in technological research in that field.
Maloney on Monday sent a letter to Greenspan, requesting files documenting the Fed's transportation operations since 1995 in view of a hearing on the matter in September.

A downsizing of Fed operations could affect thousands of the 25,000 people the Fed employs in its financial services at its 12 Federal Reserve banks which, together with the Fed Board, form the Fed System.
